say.en: One physical machine, running Linux and Windows at the same time, each convinced it owns the hardware. That is a virtual machine, and it is how the whole cloud works.
Here are the eight stages.
What a VM is, the two kinds of hypervisor, and the trick that makes it work, trap and emulate.
Then memory and I/O, the cost in numbers, and an exam question.
Stage 1: the picture. At the bottom, the real hardware.

do.text: Stage 1 of 8: what a virtual machine is

say.en: On it runs the hypervisor, also called the virtual machine monitor. It owns the real hardware.
Above it, each virtual machine runs a complete guest OS, here Linux and Windows.
And the guests run their applications, unchanged.
The hypervisor's job: give each guest the illusion of a whole machine, while keeping the guests apart.

do.text: hypervisor: one real machine → many virtual ones

say.en: Why bother? First, isolation: a crash or an attack inside one VM cannot reach another.
Consolidation: many servers that each sit mostly idle can share one machine.
Managing software: a whole OS with its applications becomes one file, to copy, snapshot and restore.
A running VM can even migrate to another machine. And all of this is what lets cloud providers rent out VMs by the hour.
Stage 2: there are two kinds of hypervisor.
Type 1, bare metal, runs directly on the hardware. Type 2, hosted, runs as an ordinary program on a host OS.
Type 1 examples: VMware ESXi, Xen, Microsoft Hyper-V. Type 2: VirtualBox, VMware Workstation.
Type 1 runs servers and the cloud. Type 2 runs on desktops, for testing and trying other systems.
And type 2 costs more, because every request from a guest also passes through the host OS.

do.text: type 1: on the hardware · type 2: on a host OS

say.en: Stage 3: how can a guest OS run at full speed, yet never take over the real machine? Trap and emulate.
The guest's applications run directly on the CPU. No interpretation, full speed.
The guest OS runs directly too, but in user mode, not kernel mode. It does not know that.
Sooner or later it executes a privileged instruction. Say, disable interrupts.
In user mode that is not allowed, so the CPU traps, and control passes to the hypervisor.
The hypervisor emulates the instruction, but only for this VM. It clears that VM's virtual interrupt flag, not the real one.
And the guest resumes, unaware. The real machine stays under the hypervisor's control.

do.text: run directly · trap the privileged instructions · emulate them

say.en: Stage 4: this only works if the right instructions trap. Popek and Goldberg stated the condition in 1974.

do.text: Stage 4 of 8: when an ISA is hard to virtualize

say.en: Every sensitive instruction must be privileged.
Sensitive means it reads or changes the machine's state. Privileged means it traps in user mode. If a sensitive instruction runs quietly in user mode, the hypervisor never sees it.
The classic x86 broke this rule. POPF, for example, run in user mode, silently ignores a change to the interrupt flag. No trap: the guest's request is simply lost.
Fix one, binary translation: the hypervisor scans the guest kernel's code and rewrites the bad instructions before they run. Early VMware did this.
Fix two, paravirtualization: change the guest OS itself to call the hypervisor directly, with hypercalls. Xen did this.
Fix three, hardware support. Intel VT-x and AMD-V add a new root mode for the hypervisor. The guest runs in its own kernel mode, and the hardware traps exactly the events the hypervisor asks for.

do.text: sensitive must be privileged · else translate, paravirtualize, or add hardware

say.en: Stage 5: memory. Now there are three kinds of address.
The guest's programs use guest virtual addresses. The guest OS page table maps them to guest physical addresses, what the guest believes is RAM.
But that is not real memory. The hypervisor maps guest physical to host physical, the real frames.
The TLB must end up holding guest virtual to host physical. Two ways to get there.
Shadow page tables: the hypervisor builds the combined table itself. But then every write the guest makes to its own page table must trap, so the shadow stays in sync.
Nested, or extended, page tables: the hardware walks both tables itself. Intel calls it EPT, AMD calls it NPT. No traps, but a TLB miss becomes expensive.
How expensive? Say the guest table has g levels and the host table h levels.
Every pointer in the guest's walk is a guest physical address, and so is the final result. That is g plus 1 addresses, and each needs its own h-level host walk.
Add the g guest reads themselves: g plus 1, times h, plus g. Which is g plus 1, times h plus 1, minus 1.
With four levels each, 24 memory references, against 4 natively. That is why large pages and big TLBs matter so much inside VMs.
Stage 6: I/O. Guests share the same disks and network cards.
The simplest: the hypervisor pretends to be a well-known device. Any guest driver works, but every device register access traps.
Faster: paravirtual drivers, such as virtio. The guest knows it is in a VM, and hands over requests in batches.
Fastest: give a real device to one VM directly. An IOMMU translates and checks the device's memory accesses, so it cannot touch other VMs.

do.text: emulate · paravirtualize · assign directly with an IOMMU

say.en: Stage 7: what does a VM cost? The answer depends on how often the guest traps.

do.text: Stage 7 of 8: the cost in numbers

say.en: A program takes 10 seconds natively, and 20 percent of that is OS work that traps in a VM. Suppose that part runs 5 times slower: 8 plus 2 times 5 is 18 seconds. A slowdown of 1.8.
With hardware support, say the OS part is only 1.5 times slower: 8 plus 3, 11 seconds.
And a pure computation hardly traps at all, so it runs at almost native speed. This is Amdahl's law again: only the part that traps is slowed.

do.text: VM time = untouched part + trapping part × its slowdown

say.en: Now an exam question.
A program runs 20 seconds natively, 30 percent of it OS work. Find its time in a VM where OS work is 4 times slower, and with hardware support, 2 times slower.

Then: memory references for one nested walk, with a 2-level guest table and a 3-level host table. And can trap and emulate handle an instruction that reads a privileged flag without trapping? Pause and work it out.
a: 70 percent, 14 seconds, is unchanged. The OS part, 6 seconds, becomes 24. 38 seconds, a slowdown of 1.9.
b: 14 plus 6 times 2: 26 seconds.
c: 2 plus 1, times 3 plus 1, minus 1. 11 references.
d: no. Reading a privileged flag makes it sensitive, and it does not trap, so it is not privileged. The hypervisor would never see it.
The usual slips: slowing down the whole program instead of only the trapping part, and forgetting the final address translation in a nested walk.

do.text: only the trapping part slows down

say.en: Let us walk the stages again.
A hypervisor runs many guest OSes on one machine. Guests run directly, and their privileged instructions trap and are emulated. That needs every sensitive instruction to be privileged.
Memory needs two translations, done by shadow or nested page tables. I/O is emulated, paravirtual, or assigned directly. And the cost is Amdahl's law on the trapping part.
